# Benchmarks

<!-- Generated by scripts/make_bench_page.py from docs/benchmarks.in.md.
     Edit the template, not docs/benchmarks.md. -->

Measured on 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12700H, Linux, GCC 15.2, 2026-11-14. Release build (`-O2`), one pinned core
(threads: eight cores). Reproduce with:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build
./build/bench_rss 2000000
./build/bench_runtime 4194304 10000 list     # or map, hash, arithmetic, ...
scripts/make_bench_page.py runtime.md rss.txt > docs/benchmarks.md
```

For a quick check on your own machine, run `./build/example_expect_gains`:
it prints memory per element and time per operation for each std
container against its cptr counterpart.

## Summary

- **Memory:** the bundled containers use half the memory of the std ones.
- **Speed:** against raw links in the same container, compressed links are
  mostly equal or faster once a structure outgrows the caches, because more
  nodes fit in each cache line and page. The exceptions: `unordered_map`
  find and erase, pointer chases that fit in L1 or L2, and the slowest
  0.5% of list walks and shrinks. The tables below give every case.
- **Where it costs:** a compressed pointer is decompressed with an add (and
  a conditional move for null). On a pointer chase that fits in L1, that
  shows; `nonnull_ptr` removes most of it. Pointer arithmetic over arrays
  does not vectorise: convert to `T*` once for hot loops.

Tails matter as much as medians: the p99 and p99.5 bars show the slowest
1% and 0.5% of epochs. Compression helps most there for structures that
outgrow the caches, because half as much memory is touched.

## Memory

Resident set growth for 2,000,000 elements, per element. "Cage, raw links"
is the same container and allocator with 8-byte links, which separates the
effect of compression from the effect of the header-less allocator.

| Structure | std | cage, raw links | cage, compressed | compressed vs std |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| list of `uint32_t` | 32.0 B | 24.1 B | **16.1 B** | −50% |
| map `uint32_t → uint32_t` | 48.0 B | 40.1 B | **24.1 B** | −50% |
| hash map `uint32_t → uint32_t` | 43.8 B | 32.6 B | **20.4 B** | −53% |
| graph, 16 edges per vertex | 168.0 B | — | **88.1 B** | −48% |

## How the time is measured

`bench_runtime` uses [nanobench](https://github.com/martinus/nanobench).
Each benchmark runs thousands of short epochs of a few hundred operations on
a structure that stays large for the whole run, and reports the 50th, 90th,
95th, 99th and 99.5th percentile of the time per element. Each variant is compared
with a reference at the same percentile: Δp99 = +10% means its p99 is 10%
slower than the reference's p99. The reference is the same container with
raw 8-byte links, or a raw `T*`. Variants run interleaved, in bursts of 8
epochs, so frequency changes and other drift affect all of them alike. Up to
p99 two runs agree within a few percent; p99.5 is the 50th-slowest of
10,000 samples and moves more.

## Linked list

*list of `uint32_t`, 4194304 elements, ns per element (chunks of 512, walk 4096)*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| grow: `cptr::list` raw links | 11.2 | 58.1 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| grow: `cptr::list` compressed | 9.77 | 53.4 | −13% | −16% | −11% | −22% | −8% |
| grow: `std::list` | 18.5 | 65.8 | +66% | +56% | +56% | +55% | +13% |
| walk: `cptr::list` raw links | 1.68 | 2.7 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| walk: `cptr::list` compressed | 1.53 | 2.45 | −9% | −10% | −12% | −14% | −9% |
| walk: `std::list` | 2.06 | 3.95 | +22% | +22% | +25% | +27% | +46% |
| shrink: `cptr::list` raw links | 7.7 | 33.7 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| shrink: `cptr::list` compressed | 8.21 | 53 | +7% | −28% | +6% | +37% | +57% |
| shrink: `std::list` | 5.3 | 15 | −31% | −63% | −64% | −50% | −55% |

The compressed list grows faster than the raw one because it commits and
touches half as much memory, and walks faster because twice as many nodes
fit in a cache line. `std::list` pops faster: glibc's `free` is cheaper
than the cage allocator's `deallocate`.

## Ordered map

*map `uint32_t -> uint32_t`, 4194304 random keys, ns per element*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| grow: `cptr::ordered_map` raw links | 731 | 1104 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| grow: `cptr::ordered_map` compressed | 718 | 1076 | −2% | −3% | −2% | −2% | −3% |
| grow: `std::map` | 817 | 1213 | +12% | +8% | +7% | +8% | +10% |
| find: `cptr::ordered_map` raw links | 829 | 1157 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| find: `cptr::ordered_map` compressed | 808 | 1151 | −2% | −2% | −2% | −1% | −1% |
| find: `std::map` | 894 | 1316 | +8% | +8% | +8% | +10% | +14% |
| walk: `cptr::ordered_map` raw links | 103 | 121 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| walk: `cptr::ordered_map` compressed | 100 | 117 | −3% | −2% | −2% | −3% | −4% |
| walk: `std::map` | 104 | 122 | +1% | +1% | +1% | +1% | +1% |
| shrink: `cptr::ordered_map` raw links | 921 | 1268 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| shrink: `cptr::ordered_map` compressed | 897 | 1252 | −3% | −2% | −1% | −1% | −1% |
| shrink: `std::map` | 882 | 1184 | −4% | −4% | −3% | −6% | −7% |

`cptr::ordered_map` is a red-black tree like `std::map`, with 24-byte
instead of 48-byte nodes for 4-byte keys and values.

## Hash map

*hash map `uint32_t -> uint32_t`, 4194304 random keys, ns per element*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| grow: `cptr::unordered_map` raw links | 93.3 | 163 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| grow: `cptr::unordered_map` compressed | 90 | 159 | −4% | −2% | −1% | −5% | −3% |
| grow: `std::unordered_map` | 108 | 187 | +16% | +13% | +14% | +17% | +14% |
| find: `cptr::unordered_map` raw links | 42.4 | 87.9 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| find: `cptr::unordered_map` compressed | 48.5 | 93.6 | +14% | +14% | +14% | +14% | +7% |
| find: `std::unordered_map` | 28.1 | 46.3 | −34% | −36% | −37% | −40% | −47% |
| walk: `cptr::unordered_map` raw links | 94.5 | 114 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| walk: `cptr::unordered_map` compressed | 92.1 | 109 | −3% | −3% | −3% | −4% | −4% |
| walk: `std::unordered_map` | 20 | 93 | −79% | −21% | −16% | −17% | −19% |
| shrink: `cptr::unordered_map` raw links | 79.2 | 139 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| shrink: `cptr::unordered_map` compressed | 80 | 146 | +1% | +8% | +7% | +4% | +5% |
| shrink: `std::unordered_map` | 106 | 168 | +34% | +23% | +22% | +25% | +21% |

These keys are 0 to n − 1, inserted in random order. `std::hash<uint32_t>` is the identity, so
`std::unordered_map` gives every such key a bucket of its own, which favours
it at find. With keys spread over the 32-bit range (as in
`example_expect_gains`), or with a mixing hash, `cptr::unordered_map` finds
as fast or faster. `std::unordered_map` keeps its nodes on one list in
allocation order, so it walks memory nearly in order; `cptr::unordered_map`
walks bucket by bucket.

## Allocator

*Allocator: free a random block of 65,536 and allocate 16 to 256 bytes, ns per free and allocate*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `malloc` / `free` | 16.3 | 49.4 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| cage `allocate` / `deallocate` | 12 | 45.5 | −26% | −39% | −44% | −31% | −8% |

*Allocator churn on several threads, ns per free and allocate on each thread*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 threads, `malloc` / `free` | 12.3 | 26.3 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 1 threads, cage | 9.84 | 15.6 | −20% | −27% | −23% | −44% | −41% |
| 2 threads, `malloc` / `free` | 10.9 | 25 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 2 threads, cage | 10.2 | 17.6 | −6% | −26% | −27% | −36% | −30% |
| 4 threads, `malloc` / `free` | 11.8 | 24.6 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 4 threads, cage | 11.2 | 20.4 | −5% | −10% | −17% | −18% | −17% |
| 8 threads, `malloc` / `free` | 24.2 | 74.2 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 8 threads, cage | 18.7 | 34.5 | −23% | −26% | −32% | −57% | −53% |

Each thread keeps a cache of up to 32 freed blocks per size class and takes
the cage's lock only to refill or flush half of it.

## Pointer chasing

A random cycle through *n* nodes. This is where the decompression add sits
on the critical path of every load.

*Pointer chasing, random cycle, 4 B payload (node 8 B compressed, 16 B raw), ns per step*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1024 nodes, raw `T*` | 1.21 | 1.83 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 1024 nodes, `ptr` | 1.86 | 2.5 | +54% | +32% | +30% | +29% | +37% |
| 1024 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 1.39 | 1.8 | +16% | +2% | +1% | +1% | −2% |
| 16384 nodes, raw `T*` | 3.12 | 3.99 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 16384 nodes, `ptr` | 3.47 | 4.35 | +11% | +12% | +11% | +6% | +9% |
| 16384 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 3.02 | 3.53 | −3% | −2% | −3% | −7% | −12% |
| 262144 nodes, raw `T*` | 14.5 | 63.2 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 262144 nodes, `ptr` | 13.7 | 39.6 | −5% | −36% | −44% | −38% | −37% |
| 262144 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 13.3 | 40 | −8% | −36% | −42% | −39% | −37% |
| 4194304 nodes, raw `T*` | 88.5 | 117 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 4194304 nodes, `ptr` | 82.9 | 114 | −6% | −3% | −3% | −4% | −2% |
| 4194304 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 82.3 | 113 | −7% | −3% | −3% | −5% | −3% |

*Pointer chasing, random cycle, 56 B payload (node 60 B compressed, 64 B raw), ns per step*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1024 nodes, raw `T*` | 3.29 | 4.22 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 1024 nodes, `ptr` | 3.78 | 4.71 | +15% | +16% | +15% | +15% | +12% |
| 1024 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 3.34 | 4.24 | +2% | +3% | +3% | +1% | +1% |
| 16384 nodes, raw `T*` | 14 | 28.3 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 16384 nodes, `ptr` | 14.1 | 26.3 | +0% | −0% | +0% | −1% | −7% |
| 16384 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 13.7 | 18.1 | −2% | −3% | −3% | −32% | −36% |
| 262144 nodes, raw `T*` | 85 | 115 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 262144 nodes, `ptr` | 83.4 | 114 | −2% | −1% | −1% | −1% | −1% |
| 262144 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 81.7 | 111 | −4% | −2% | −1% | −3% | −3% |
| 4194304 nodes, raw `T*` | 99.6 | 130 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 4194304 nodes, `ptr` | 99.9 | 134 | +0% | +0% | +1% | +1% | +3% |
| 4194304 nodes, `nonnull_ptr` | 99.4 | 132 | −0% | −0% | −1% | −0% | +1% |

In L1 and L2 the add and the null check show; `nonnull_ptr` has no null
check and costs much less. From L3 on, the smaller nodes win.

## Pointer arithmetic and conversions

*Pointer arithmetic: `++p` over an array of `uint32_t`, ns per element*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 65536 elements, raw `T*` | 0.09 | 0.12 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 65536 elements, `ptr` | 0.31 | 0.36 | +234% | +234% | +232% | +223% | +199% |
| 4194304 elements, raw `T*` | 0.17 | 1.22 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| 4194304 elements, `ptr` | 0.31 | 0.39 | +85% | +41% | +35% | +19% | −68% |

The raw loop is vectorised. A 32-bit offset that may wrap is not an
induction variable the compiler can turn into a pointer, so the `ptr` loop
stays scalar. In a hot loop over an array, convert to `T*` once with
`get()`.

*Conversion of 4,096 `ptr<int>`, ns per conversion*

|  | p50 ns | p99.5 ns | Δp50 | Δp90 | Δp95 | Δp99 | Δp99.5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| copy to `ptr<int>` | 0.09 | 0.11 | ref | ref | ref | ref | ref |
| to `ptr<const int>` | 0.09 | 0.11 | +2% | +0% | +1% | +1% | +1% |
| to `ptr<void>` | 0.09 | 0.11 | +2% | +0% | +2% | +0% | +0% |
